# STOCHASTIC PHENOTYPES IN RAS-DEPENDENT DEVELOPMENTAL DISEASES

**Authors:** Robert A. Marmion; Alison G. Simpkins; Lena A. Barrett; David W. Denberg; Susan Zusman; Jodi Schottenfeld-Roames; Trudi Schüpbach; Stanislav Y. Shvartsman

**Affiliations:** 1Lewis-Sigler Institute for Integrative Genomics, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08544, USA. | 2Department of Chemical and Biological Engineering, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08544, USA. | 3Department of Molecular Biology, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08544, USA. | 4Flatiron Institute, Simons Foundation, New York, NY 10010, USA.

## Abstract

Germline mutations upregulating RAS signaling are associated with multiple developmental disorders. A hallmark of these conditions is that the same mutation may present vastly different phenotypes in different individuals, even in monozygotic twins. Here we demonstrate how the origins of such largely unexplained phenotypic variations may be dissected using highly controlled studies in Drosophila that have been gene-edited to carry activating variants of MEK, a core enzyme in the RAS pathway. This allowed us to measure the small, but consistent increase in signaling output of such alleles in vivo. The fraction of mutation carriers reaching adulthood was strongly reduced, but most surviving animals had normal RAS-dependent structures. We rationalize these results using a stochastic signaling model and support it by quantifying cell fate specification errors in bilaterally symmetric larval trachea, a RAS-dependent structure that allows us to isolate the effects of mutations from potential contributions of genetic modifiers and environmental differences. We propose that the small increase in signaling output shifts the distribution of phenotypes into a regime, where stochastic variation causes defects in some individuals, but not in others. Our findings shed light on phenotypic heterogeneity of developmental disorders caused by deregulated RAS signaling and offer a framework for investigating causal effects of other pathogenic alleles and mild mutations in general.

## Abstract

High phenotypic variability in developmental diseases associated with RAS pathway mutations is commonly explained by modifier genes and environmental effects. Marmion et al. use gene editing and analysis of fluctuating asymmetry in Drosophila to demonstrate that phenotypic variability can have stochastic origins.

## Introduction

Germline mutations in cell signaling genes can cause severe developmental abnormalities. For example, activating mutations in members of the Fibroblast Growth Factor Receptor (FGFR) family are causally linked to craniofacial and limb defects in Crouzon, Apert, and Pfeifer syndromes 1–3. Another class of developmental diseases, known as the RASopathies, is associated with germline mutations within the RAS cascade, which transmits signals from ligand-activated FGFR and other cell surface receptors 4,5. Carriers of these mutations can display a spectrum of morphological and functional phenotypes, including heart defects, craniofacial dysmorphisms, stunted growth, and neurocognitive delays. While the discovery of mutations associated with this class of developmental syndromes and their molecular characterization is proceeding at an ever-increasing pace, understanding of the emerging developmental phenotypes remains rudimentary. Here, we focus on the widely recognized but poorly understood observation that the same mutation can have vastly different effects on different individuals, with discordant phenotypes appearing even in monozygotic twins 6–8.

Phenotypic variations associated with mutations in cell signaling genes are known to both clinicians, who continue to report strikingly different severity of structural and functional defects in carriers of the same mutation, and to developmental geneticists, who commonly observe variable phenotypes in model organisms. This is particularly true for so called “mild” alleles and is not surprising given that the effects of a germline mutation can be impacted by genetic background, environmental conditions, somatic mosaicism, and by the intrinsic stochasticity of molecular processes. Disentangling these contributions requires studies in large cohorts of organisms with precisely controlled genotypes and carefully controlled environmental conditions. We carried out such an investigation in Drosophila, a model organism that played a key role in the discovery of the RAS cascade.

Previous work investigating human disease variants in Drosophila was largely based on misexpression systems, which usually lead to strongly skewed gene dosages, making them incompatible with normal development 9,10. A new suite of gene editing tools allowed us to sidestep this problem and study organism-level effects of disease mutations in heterozygous and homozygous conditions, with statistical power not readily matched by studies in vertebrates 11. Capitalizing on these advantages, we used several well-understood RAS-dependent developmental events to quantify the effects of mutations affecting a core kinase in the RAS cascade. A major finding is the discovery of a clear stochastic contribution to the observed variations of developmental phenotypes, with direct implications for both fundamental and clinical understanding of the underlying mechanisms.

## Results

### Pathogenic MEK variants cause morphological defects in the RAS-dependent adult structures

The MAP2K1 gene in humans encodes MEK1, a core component of the RAS pathway. Wild type MEK1 (henceforth, just MEK) is a ubiquitously expressed enzyme which is activated, by phosphorylation, when the pathway is stimulated by ligand-bound cell surface receptors. Active MEK dually phosphorylates and thereby activates its only known substrate, ERK, a kinase with many substrates involved in control of critical cellular functions 12,13. MEK is deregulated by mutations in multiple diseases, including developmental disorders and cancers. A large number of these mutations, which are found along the length of the protein, are listed in the ClinVar database (Figure 1A and 1B). We selected three alleles that correspond to missense mutations: two variants, F53S and Y130C, were identified by studies of Cardiofaciocutaneous syndrome (CFCS) 14,15, a member of the RASopathies; the E203K variant was identified in melanoma 16. In contrast to wild type MEK, all three variants display small levels of ligand-independent kinase activity and are more readily activated by signaling from ligand-bound receptor tyrosine kinases 17. To determine how these molecular-level changes play out during development, we used CRISPR-Cas9 to introduce the corresponding mutations into the endogenous Drosophila Dsor1 gene, which encodes a homologue of MEK and mediates all RAS-dependent processes in the fly 18.

The scarless gene editing approach allowed us to generate fly lines with only two single-nucleotide changes in the genome: a PAM mutation together with a coding non-synonymous substitution corresponding to each of the three chosen MEK variants 19–21. We established homozygous flies for each of the three substitutions and proceeded to examine their effects on development (Figure 1C, 1D, and S1), starting with the RAS-dependent patterning of the adult structures. For instance, the bipartite Gal4-UAS system has been extensively used to study the effects of constitutively active RAS pathway components on the wing and eye patterning. Targeted expression of these components in the wing and eye imaginal discs induces multiple ectopic wing veins in the adult wing and causes a “rough eye” phenotype 22–24. In contrast to these strong effects, we found that the adult wings and eyes of the flies with the gene edited endogenous MEK locus had only mild patterning defects. Only a small fraction of wings (~10%) had ectopic posterior cross-veins, which can be compared to a higher penetrance of ectopic veins caused by misexpression of the same MEK variants (Figure 1E and 1F). The patterning of the adult eye was also largely normal (Figure 1G and 1H). The average number of nearest neighbors in the array of photoreceptors was still six, but the variance of the number of nearest neighbors was significantly increased.

The incomplete penetrance and variable expressivity of the ectopic wing and rough eye phenotypes suggest that the introduced mutations cause modest changes of ERK activation. To test this, we turned to the early embryo, where the RAS pathway is engaged by a locally activated Torso receptor tyrosine kinase, in a developmental context where endogenous ERK activation can be accurately quantified and compared between genetic backgrounds. ERK activation is normally present only at the poles, reflecting the localized release of the ligand that binds to uniformly expressed Torso. This pattern is affected only slightly in embryos carrying the pathogenic MEK variants (Figure 2). Specifically, we detected ERK activation in the middle of the embryo of both variants, where ERK is normally inactive, as well as higher levels of ERK activation at the poles of E203K. While both of these changes are statistically significant, they are small in magnitude. We expect this to be a general feature of ERK signaling in homozygous and heterozygous carriers of mutations associated with the RAS-dependent developmental disorders.

### Embryonic lethality caused by pathogenic MEK variants requires RTK activation

The difference between the somatic RAS pathway mutations from cancers, which are believed to be embryonic lethal, and the germline mutations from developmental abnormalities, which are compatible with development, might be quantitative, translated into the difference in the fraction of individuals that reach adulthood. To explore this option in our experiments, we turned to the F53S line and followed the developmental progression in cohorts of homozygous embryos. A large fraction of embryos (~50%) failed to hatch (Figure 3A and 3B). The embryonic lethality varied among the three variants, consistent with their differential severity reported by earlier overexpression studies 10. Moreover, lethality and the developmental delay effect were not limited to embryogenesis, as only a fraction (~60%) of homozygous larvae became pupae (Figure 3A and 3C). Thus, activating mutations drastically reduce the probability of reaching adulthood.

Since RAS is involved in most steps of development, tracking the origins of developmental delays and lethality is not a trivial task, but it is made easier by earlier genetic studies. Midway through oogenesis, a region of the follicular epithelium is patterned by Gurken (Grk), a protein that is secreted from the oocyte and activates the Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor (EGFR) tyrosine kinase on the follicle cells 25. Acting through the RAS cascade in the follicle cells, EGFR signaling induces two identical appendage primordia, which are positioned at the intermediated levels of the single-peaked pattern of EGFR activation by Grk and give rise to two respiratory eggshell appendages. Perturbing the sensitivity of the follicle cells to Grk alters inter-appendage spacing, with increase/decrease of this spacing corresponding to higher/lower levels of the Grk-dependent RAS signaling 26. We therefore started our analysis by examining the spacing between the respiratory eggshell appendages. We found that eggshell appendages from both heterozygous and homozygous F53S females were significantly further apart than in wild type controls (Figure 4A). Thus, activating mutations cause morphologically significant signaling changes in vivo.

Grk-induced RAS signaling represses a sulfotransferase-encoding gene pipe (pip), restricting its expression to the ventral domain of the follicular epithelium 27,28. This is the first step in a cascade specifying the ventral cell fates in the embryo 29–32. Similar to the distance between the eggshell appendages, the expression domain of pip is sensitive to genetic perturbations of RAS signaling in the follicular epithelium. Studies with genetic mosaics established that when follicle cells are sensitized to low-levels of Grk, the pip domain is disrupted, which causes clear defects in patterning of the ventral side of the embryo. Since the disease alleles of MEK are more sensitive to activation by RTKs, we reasoned that the same effects should be present in our embryos 33,34. We confirmed this prediction by visualizing the domain of Snail (Sna), a zygotically expressed Zn-finger transcription factor, which is normally expressed in a continuous ventral domain. The Sna domain in a fraction of blastoderm-stage embryos (3/11) was disrupted, which implies that the ventral follicle cells with the F53S MEK variant have abnormally high levels of RAS signaling (Figure 4B and 4C). Furthermore, consistent with the known connection between ovarian RAS signaling and early embryogenesis, some dead embryos (~10%) had defects characteristic of disrupted ventral patterning (Figure 4D and 4E). Several aspects of embryonic lethality of the F53S flies may therefore stem from increased levels of the Grk-induced RAS signaling in oogenesis. We tested this possibility genetically, by placing F53S MEK in females with only one copy of Grk. The embryonic lethality was dramatically reduced, from ~40% to ~20%, which is only slightly above lethality in controls (Figure 4F). This strongly suggests that developmental defects caused by pathogenic MEK variants require the presence of extracellular inputs to the RAS pathway.

### Stochastic model for observed phenotypic variations

Variable phenotypes in Mendelian disorders are commonly attributed to the effects of modifier genes and environmental factors. While these important factors are impossible to exclude even in experiments with inbred flies, we note that at least some aspects of phenotypic variability can be of stochastic origin. The following conceptual model can account for most of our observations: Each of these RAS-dependent events along a developmental trajectory is triggered by an extracellular input which is interpreted by an intracellular signaling network. The outcome of each signaling event depends both on the extracellular input to the intracellular network and on its sensitivity to this input. In the simplest case, it is a product of these two factors (Figure 5) 35. We assume that the input strength is variable, reflecting the combined effects of multiple steps in the synthesis, processing, and secretion of extracellular ligands. The sensitivity of the wild type system is tuned such that for most individuals the signaling outcome is below a threshold leading to a patterning or morphogenetic defect. In the presence of mutations that cause a small increase in signaling sensitivity, the fraction of individuals where this threshold is crossed will be higher. However, individuals with lower values of input will not cross the threshold even in the presence of a sensitizing mutation. The same model applies to each of the RAS-dependent events. For some of these events, crossing the threshold will give rise to a defect that is compatible with further development, such a cell-fate specification event leading to an ectopic wing vein. For others, the outcome will be catastrophic and terminate development.

While the effects of halving the Grk level support the proposed stochastic explanation for incomplete penetrance of lethality caused by activating mutations, one can always object that different individuals are not truly identical, even when resulting from highly inbred lines. An independent line of reasoning is based on analyzing the variations in the formation of the RAS-dependent bilateral structures within a single individual, such as the terminal cells in the larval tracheal system. Terminal cells supply directly adjacent tissues with oxygen, which arrives by diffusion through the elaborate tracheal network 36. Located at symmetric positions within each metamere of the animal, each terminal cell (Figure 6A–C) is selected from a multicellular primordium during embryogenesis in response to high levels of FGF 36. Most extensively studied in the dorsal terminal cells, the selection process is initiated by the limiting amounts of the FGF ligand Branchless, which requires intracellular feedbacks and lateral inhibition circuits to ensure that only one cell within the primordium acquires the terminal fate 37. For instance, disruption of the Sprouty-dependent negative feedback loop within the RAS pathway leads to the occasional formation of ectopic terminal cells, uncovering variations in the FGF-dependent input to each primordium 38. While these cells eventually pair up on the dorsal side of the embryo, the initial patterning event occurs in two distant cell clusters on either side of the embryo.

Since the wild type system is tuned to operate with normal MEK, we reasoned that it may be placed outside of its normal operating regime by the activating MEK variants 17. Specifically, we predicted that mildly activating mutations might cause mistakes to occur randomly in some instances of the terminal cell selection process, as is observed in the absence of Sprouty. Consistent with this expectation, our analysis of both F53S and E203K larvae revealed the formation of ectopic terminal cells (Figure 6D and 6E). In contrast to wild type larvae, with symmetrically positioned individual terminal cells, there are larvae with up to 5 terminal cells in a single metamere. Since two independent cell populations respond to RAS signaling and later merge to form a single metamere, we tested a probabilistic model for induction of ectopic terminal cells on either side of the larva (Figure 6F and 6G). By examining ectopic dorsal terminal cells from F53S larvae, we observed 196 metameres. There were 22 instances of single ectopic terminal cells on the left, 23 on the right, and 6 on both sides. The chance of finding defects on both sides is 14.8%2 or 2.2%. This is consistent with the observed 6/196 or 3.1%. We found a similar random distribution of ectopic terminal cells in E203K larvae. Thus, ectopic cells were distributed randomly on the two sides of larvae, consistent with the model whereby activating mutations uncover variations of the endogenous input to the RAS pathway. As a final test of the random distribution of defects, we returned to the wings of F53S females (Figure 6H and 6I). We found that most adults had only one wing with an ectopic posterior crossvein, and the expected distribution was strikingly similar to random.

## Discussion

Making the most of the rapidly accumulating personalized sequencing data in the RASopathies and related disorders requires strategies for causal studies of pathogenic mutations at multiple levels of biological organization. Previous studies used biochemical assays and overexpression approaches to characterize molecular effects of pathogenic mutations 9,17,39–41. However, analyzing their effects in the organism requires quantitative studies in large cohorts of homozygous and heterozygous mutation carriers. Our studies with gene-edited Drosophila established that homozygous and heterozygous carriers of pathogenic MEK variants display statistically significant, but small changes in ERK activation and that these changes cause partially penetrant phenotypes, including cell fate specification defects, embryonic lethality, and developmental delays. The presented approach can be readily applied to other mutations and can be used to probe the variability of other RAS-dependent phenotypes, such as learning, memory, and metabolism 42,43.

We proposed that the observed phenotypic variability stems from stochastic variations in the levels of RTK ligands that trigger the RAS pathway in carriers of mutations that sensitize the pathway to extracellular cues. Future tests of this model require measurements of RTK signaling inputs in multiple stages of development. However, already at this point our model is strongly supported by statistical characterization of fluctuating asymmetries of bilaterally symmetric structures, such as the terminal cells in the larval trachea. Our within-subject analysis does not mean that genetic modifiers and environmental differences do not contribute to the variability of other phenotypes, such as embryonic lethality and developmental delays, However, it strongly argues that genetic modifiers and environmental differences are not the sole contributors to the phenotypic variability in carriers of the RAS pathway mutations.

Among developmental mutations in model organisms, it is well established that milder mutations tend to be more variable than the so called “strong” mutations that cause more consistent phenotypes. With the smaller shifts in signaling, the intrinsic variability of the signaling processes will shift outcomes into a regime where some individuals still are in the normal range, whereas others will show a phenotype. Only if the mutation causes a substantial shift away from the normal mean, will a consistent mutant phenotype occur. These considerations should play an important role in establishing quantitative understanding of the genotype-to-phenotype associations in a large class of developmental abnormalities.

We close by offering a quantitative perspective on the penetrance of developmental phenotypes caused by genetically deregulated signaling: discovery of de novo mutations associated with diseases like CFCS and other RASopathies prompted studies on whether the presence of such mutations is sufficient for disrupting development in all mutation carriers. Since the RAS-dependent structures are normal in a significant fraction of adult flies with two copies of a pathogenic mutation, the answer appears to be negative. This implies that although some individuals possessing disease mutations do survive to adulthood, there is a substantial amount of embryonic lethality that would presumably go undetected. Furthermore, survivors that do reach adulthood may do so because of random signaling fluctuations at critical points in development. Our findings would therefore predict the existence of individuals that have a mutation but display no overt phenotypes. This prediction is consistent with a study of thousands of UK Biobank exomes that concluded that a large fraction of carriers do not present features of the RASopathies and thus remain undiagnosed 44.

### METHODS DETAILS

#### Fly stocks

Our genome editing strategy resulted in just two single-point mutations in the Drosophila genome. The strategy requires the creation of a stable non-expressing (“off”) line. This stable fly line would introduce the SNP causing F53S by inserting the sequence change into the Drosophila Dsor1 locus, together with a positive selection cassette, via Homology Directed Repair (HDR) following site-specific cleavage of genomic DNA by Cas9 19–21. We utilized a scarless genome editing strategy, which inserts the sequence change into a targeted site together with a positive selection cassette, via Homology Directed Repair (HDR), following site-specific cleavage of genomic DNA by the Cas9 endonuclease. The HDR donor plasmid contains a 3xP3 promoter driven dsRed marker flanked by PiggyBac (PBac) transposase recognition sites, as well as 1 kb homology arms for HDR. One of the arms has the desired mutation, which is incorporated into the targeted gene upon repair (Figure S1). To prevent repeated cleavage following HDR, the targeted protospacer motif (PAM) site in the donor plasmid is also mutated (Figure S1). Following injection of the HDR plasmid and the guide RNA (gRNA) into embryos expressing Cas9, adult progeny were screened for the expression of dsRed in their eyes (Figure S1). The dsRed cassette, inserted into the intron of the targeted gene, served a dual function: providing an easily visualized marker while truncating the target gene product and preventing lethality/sterility that may be caused by the introduced mutation. Thus, once a transformed line is created, the insertion can be maintained in a stable line over a balancer chromosome, which provides a wild type gene copy. We successfully created the “off” line of MEKF53S via CRISPR-HDR and confirmed by Sanger sequencing.

We subsequently activated MEKF53S by inducing germline clones, which flipped out the positive selection cassette, allowing for full-length gene expression (Figure S1). This was accomplished by crossing females from the balanced lines to males that express PiggyBac (PBac) transposase under the control of the germline-specific (nanos) promoter, as well as a balancer X chromosome. The progeny was therefore heterozygous for the balancer chromosome and the inserted sequence (Figure S1). Females containing the inserted element, the balancer chromosome, and nos-PBac were crossed to wild type males to facilitate screening of the next generation. During oogenesis, PBac transposase can flip out the dsRed cassette (with some frequency), allowing for inheritance of the mutant allele. The embryos in which recombination did not occur will inherit a truncated reading frame and truncated MEK protein (Figure S1). Since mek is on the X-chromosome and is necessary for viability, only the surviving males will carry the desired mutant allele, allowing us to directly test its effects in the organism (Figure S1). The CRISPR-HDR vector for F53S mek was created by cloning ~1Kb HDR arms into the vector pHD-ScarlessDsRed (https://flycrispr.org/) digested with AarI and SapI, via 4-piece Gibson assembly with Q5 HiFi assembly master mix together with left and right arms PCR amplified from gDNA. The sgRNA for F53S was annealed and ligated into a BbsI digested chiRNA plasmid. This site was mutated in the HDR arm to prevent cutting by Cas9 with PCR mutagenesis. F53S was introduced by PCR mutagenesis of the HDR vector. The same HDR vector and gRNA were used for Y130C, except that a different mutagenic primer was used to introduce the Y130C coding variant.

The HDR vector for E203K was assembled into pHD-scarlessDsRed using different primer pairs for the left and right arms. The sgRNA for E203K was annealed and ligated into a BbsI digested chiRNA plasmid. This site was mutated in the HDR arm to prevent cutting by Cas9 with PCR mutagenesis. E203K was introduced by PCR mutagenesis of the HDR vector. Bestgene performed injections of pairs of guideRNA vector and HDR vector. The positive selection cassette was removed using a fly expressing nos::PBac 45. PAM control lines are sister lines of the injections that failed to incorporate the coding variant but do contain the PAM mutation. Importantly, each line was confirmed by PCR amplified out of both heterozygous females and hemizygous males using outside primers and verified by sanger sequencing. The newly developed fly lines are available upon request. All egg lays, crosses, and embryonic development were conducted at 25°C.

#### Eye Graph Construction

Fly heads were immobilized onto double stick tape and imaged on a Leica M125 C stereo microscope. 30 manual optical sections were captured for each eye. Alignment was performed using 3D image registration in FIJI 46. The 3D extended depth of field algorithm in FIJI was utilized to merge optical sections. Facets in the eye images are segmented using the Flynotyper ImageJ plugin on locally enhanced contrast (CLAHE) images used as input 47. The Flynotyper segmentation output is hand-corrected and the facets far from the eye center are excluded with a mask. A graph is created by computing the voronoi tessellation of cell centers, and facets are considered adjacent if their corresponding voronoi polygons share an edge. In measuring the degree frequency, boundary nodes are excluded to capture the bulk distribution.

#### Embryonic lethality

Embryonic lethality was accessed by counting unhatched eggs that had been aged for more than 48 hours.

#### Hatch rate and pupation rate

1-hour long batch collection of eggs were monitored under oil, stage selected and moved to a fresh apple plate, monitored by video at 2-minute intervals using a Leica M125 C stereo microscope. L1 larvae were then moved to food vials at 26 hours (AEL) and monitored for pupation on 4-hour intervals. The collection of L1 larvae included larvae from the same egg collection that were not video monitored for egg hatching but includes both control and mutant larvae from the same collection/environment.

Statistical analysis was conducted using Oasis 2 by substituting mortality of individuals with progression to the next developmental stage 48. Displayed developmental progression does include all experimental individuals but statistics are performed after censoring individuals that never progress to the next developmental stage.

#### Cuticle phenotyping

Embryos were dechorionated after being aged for more than 24 h as previously reported 9,49. Dechorionated embryos were incubated overnight in a media containing lactic acid and Hoyer’s media (1:1) at 65°C. Embryos were imaged on a Nikon Eclipse Ni in darkfield.

#### Tracheal metamere quantification

Larvae that express UAS-fluorophores under control of breathless (btl-GAL4) are obtained by crossing males containing btl>GAL4, UAS-GFP, UAS-NLS-dsRed to homozygous females mutant for mekF53S or mekE203K and examining hemizygous males. To prepare samples, we followed an improved version of the rapid protocol described by others 50. Late (wandering) L3 larvae were identified by their presence on the side of vials, as early L3 and younger larvae burrow into food 51. Larvae were collected and washed with water to remove adherent yeast 52. Larvae were heat-killed at 70 °C until movement ceased (<10 s), sexed by examining gonads, mounted dorsal-side up on a glass slide in a drop of 60% v/v glycerol (ThermoFisher 17904), and covered with a #1.5 square glass coverslip. Coverslips were sealed with clear nail polish and left to dry for at least ten minutes in darkness to prevent degradation of endogenous fluorescent signal 52. Samples were imaged as soon as possible because heat-fixed trachea degrade and endogenous fluorescent signal weakens over time 50. After confocal imaging, the number of terminal cells was manually counted. A cell was only counted if it 1. had a branched morphology and 2. contained a nuclear signal outside of the dorsal branch.

#### Signaling threshold conceptual model simulation

To generate the stimulus distributions for both cases, 5000 normally distributed random values were generated and plotted using the MATLAB functions randn and histogram, respectively. The same procedure was used to produce the histogram for the case of wild type pathway sensitivity. The phenotypic distribution for the wild type case was generated by element-wise multiplication of the vectors containing stimulus and sensitivity values and subsequently plotted using the histogram function. The threshold for a mutant phenotype in this wild type phenotypic distribution was set at the x value corresponding to the 97th percentile of the phenotypic value dataset using the prctile function in MATLAB. To produce the phenotypic distribution corresponding to the MEK gain-of-function case, the mutant threshold was kept at the same x value, and the phenotypic distribution was shifted to the right until the threshold was at the value corresponding to the 73rd percentile of the phenotypic value dataset. Finally, the MEK GOF sensitivity distribution was generated by dividing the phenotypic vector by the stimulus vector in an element-by-element manner. The thresholds for mutant cutoffs are arbitrary but correspond roughly to the unaffected fraction of tracheal metameres in controls and mutants.

#### Embryo immunostaining

Antibody staining for Snail (SNA) was performed as described previously 9. Guinea pig anti-SNA (1:1000, a gift from Eric Wieschaus) was used as the primary antibody. DAPI (1:10,000; Invitrogen #D1306) was used to stain for nuclei, and Alexa Fluor conjugates (1:500; Invitrogen) were used as secondary antibodies.

#### Microscopy and image processing

Fluorescent imaging of fixed embryos for immunostaining was performed on a Nikon A1-RS or Leica SP5 scanning confocal microscope with a 20x objective, as in previously reported procedures 9. For pairwise comparisons of WT and mutant backgrounds, embryos were collected, stained, and imaged together under the same experimental conditions. Our software allows the dpERK measurements to be quantified while the experimenter is blinded to the genotype. Broken embryos, embryos with intact vitelline membrane, or embryos undergoing mitosis were excluded from the analysis.

Fluorescent imaging of heat-fixed larvae was performed on a Leica SP5 scanning confocal microscope with a 20x objective. Autofluorescence from luminal chitin was captured using the 405 nm laser 51. In addition, photomicrographs were acquired to visualize gas-filled lumens. Typically, 10x or 20x objectives are best for imaging terminal cells 50. Before taking fluorescence micrographs, the dorsal terminal cells of each larva were closely examined to ensure that the dorsal anastomoses in Tr2-Tr9 were intact. Disconnected dorsal anastomoses signal that the larva is about to pupate 53 and caused larvae to be rejected for further processing.
